definition.text: A geographically distributed network of proxy servers and data centers that delivers content to users from locations close to them.

facts.text: CDNs provide high availability and performance by placing content geographically closer to end users, and arose in the late 1990s to relieve the Internet's performance bottlenecks.
CDNs now serve a large portion of Internet content: web text, graphics and scripts, downloadable files, applications, live and on-demand streaming media, and social media services.
Static files such as HTML, CSS and JavaScript, photos and videos are generally the content served from a CDN, though a CDN can also deliver dynamic content.
Users fetch content from a nearby CDN node instead of the origin server, so the origin's servers do not have to handle the requests the CDN fulfills.
A visitor in the UK to a site hosted in the USA is served from a close edge location such as London, which is much quicker than a full request to the origin.
Benefits include reduced bandwidth costs, faster page loads, higher global availability and redundancy, and better security, notably protection against DDoS attacks.
Content owners pay CDN operators to deliver their content, and the CDN in turn pays ISPs, carriers and network operators for hosting its servers in their data centers.
Drawbacks: a CDN can be expensive for high-traffic services, some organizations and countries block popular CDN domains or IPs, and an audience far from any CDN server may see data travel farther.

definition.text: The origin server holds the original content, and edge servers are the many caching servers spread around the world that serve users nearby.

facts.text: The origin server is the primary source of content and holds its original versions, while the edge servers that cache and serve it are numerous and distributed across the world.
A CDN caches content in many geographic locations called edge locations, and each edge location holds several caching servers that deliver content to visitors in its proximity.
Providers serve a defined set of points of presence (PoPs) chosen for the coverage wanted, such as the United States, Asia-Pacific or global; these are also called edges, edge nodes or edge networks.
A CDN's footprint is the geographic area where its edge servers can effectively serve clients' requests.
CDN size varies: some have thousands of nodes and tens of thousands of servers on many remote PoPs, while others build a global network with only a small number of geographical PoPs.
CDN entry points are the servers that fetch content from the origin, and an origin shield is a CDN service that protects the origin server during heavy traffic.
DNS resolves the domain name to the IP address of the nearest edge server, and a control plane configures and manages the edge servers.

definition.text: A user's request is answered from the nearest edge server's cache, or the edge fetches the content from the origin, stores a copy and delivers it.

facts.text: After DNS resolution, the user's device sends its content request to the CDN edge server.
The edge server checks its local cache for the content and, if it finds it, serves it to the user.
If the content is not in the cache, the edge server forwards the request to the origin server.
After receiving the content from the origin, the edge server stores a copy in its cache and delivers it to the user.
Once static assets are cached at a location, later requests there are served from its edge servers instead of the origin, reducing origin load and improving scalability.
For streaming media, the CDN receives the stream at its origin server and replicates it to many or all of its edge cache servers, so HTTP streaming costs about the same as HTTP web caching.

definition.text: CDNs are divided into push CDNs, which are sent new content whenever it changes, and pull CDNs, which fetch content from the origin when a user first requests it.

facts.text: A push CDN receives new content whenever it changes on the server; the site owner uploads content directly to the CDN and rewrites URLs to point to it.
With a push CDN the owner configures when content expires and when it is updated.
Push CDNs upload content only when it is new or changed, which minimizes traffic but maximizes storage, and content is placed once instead of re-pulled at regular intervals.
Push CDNs suit sites with little traffic or with content that is not often updated.
In a pull CDN the cache is updated on request: if the CDN lacks an asset, it fetches it from the origin, populates its cache and sends the asset to the user.
Pull CDNs need less maintenance than push CDNs, because cache updates on CDN nodes happen in response to client requests.
Pull CDNs suit heavy-traffic sites, since traffic is spread more evenly and only recently requested content remains on the CDN.
In general, web caches are populated from user requests (pull caching) or from preloaded content disseminated by content servers (push caching).

definition.text: Request routing directs each client request to the content source best able to serve it, such as the closest node or the one with the most capacity.

facts.text: Request routing directs a client request to the content source best able to serve it, such as the service node closest to the client or the one with the most capacity.
Routing algorithms include global server load balancing, DNS-based request routing, dynamic metafile generation, HTML rewriting and anycasting.
Global server load balancing (GSLB) routes requests by factors such as geographic proximity, server load and network conditions.
Anycast DNS lets multiple servers share the same IP address and helps route incoming traffic to the nearest data center.
Proximity, meaning the closest service node, is estimated by reactive probing, proactive probing and connection monitoring.
Choosing for performance picks the fewest hops, shortest time to the client or highest server performance; choosing for cost picks the cheapest locations. Edge servers near users tend to win on both.
CDN providers establish a presence at major Internet Exchange Points so they can exchange traffic directly with ISPs and other networks.

definition.text: A CDN is an intelligent overlay on the Internet's simple core network that combines web caching, server-load balancing, request routing and content services.

facts.text: The Internet follows the end-to-end principle: intelligence sits at the hosts and clients, so the core network is simplified to only forward data packets.
CDNs extend the transport network with intelligent applications, forming a tightly integrated overlay that uses web caching, server-load balancing, request routing and content services.
Web caches store popular content on servers close to the greatest demand, reducing bandwidth requirements and server load and improving client response times.
Server-load balancing shares traffic among servers or web caches, for example with a layer 4-7 switch holding one virtual IP address, adding capacity, scalability, reliability and health checks.

title: End-user mapping with EDNS client subnet
article: Content delivery network#CDN trends > Improving CDN performance using Extension Mechanisms for DNS

definition.text: End-user mapping lets a CDN use the client's subnet, passed in the edns-client-subnet DNS option, to pick a nearby edge server.

facts.text: CDNs traditionally located a client by the IP of its recursive DNS resolver, which gives poor performance when the client uses a non-local resolver that is far away.
A CDN may route a client in India to its edge server in Singapore because that client uses a public DNS resolver in Singapore.

With the edns-client-subnet EDNS0 option, CDNs use the IP address of the requesting client's subnet when resolving DNS requests; this end-user mapping drastically reduces round-trip latencies for clients on non-local resolvers.
EDNS0 has drawbacks: it reduces the effectiveness of caching resolutions at recursive resolvers, increases total DNS resolution traffic, and raises a privacy concern by exposing the client's subnet.

title: Peer-to-peer CDN
article: Content delivery network#Content networking techniques > Peer-to-peer CDNs

definition.text: A peer-to-peer CDN is one in which clients provide resources as well as use them.

facts.text: In a peer-to-peer CDN clients provide resources as well as use them; CDN offloading is the mechanism that lets clients help deliver content to each other in addition to edge server delivery.
Unlike client-server systems, a peer-to-peer content network can perform better as more users access the content, especially with protocols such as BitTorrent that require users to share.
This property makes the setup and running costs very small for the original content distributor.
Web3 and blockchain technologies can incentivize peers to participate: nodes that take part receive crypto tokens in exchange for their involvement.

title: Private CDN
article: Content delivery network#Content networking techniques > Private CDNs

definition.text: A private CDN is a content delivery network built by a content owner, made of PoPs that serve content only for that owner.

facts.text: Content owners unsatisfied with the options or costs of a commercial CDN can build a private CDN, made of PoPs that only serve content for their owner.
The PoPs of a private CDN can be caching servers, reverse proxies or application delivery controllers, and it can be as simple as two caching servers or large enough to serve petabytes of content.
A private CDN deployed within a company network is also called an enterprise CDN or eCDN.
Large CDNs may build their own private network to distribute copies of content across cache locations, and use public networks as backup when its capacity is insufficient or reduced by a failure.

title: Multi-CDN
article: Content delivery network#CDN trends > Multi CDN and CDN selection

definition.text: Multi-CDN means a content provider combines several CDN services instead of relying on a single one.

facts.text: Combining several CDN services lets a content provider avoid relying on a single CDN, especially to handle high peak audiences during live events.
Traffic can be allocated among the CDNs on the client side, on the server side at the content provider's origin, or on the cloud side between the origin and the audience.
CDN selection criteria can be performance, availability and cost; a CDN selector is the decision-making service that chooses among multiple CDNs.
The IETF standardized a framework and request-routing interface for interconnecting CDNs so a request can be redirected between them; Open Caching APIs let a provider use several CDNs consistently.

title: Telco CDN
article: Content delivery network#CDN trends > Telco CDN advantages

definition.text: A telco CDN is a content delivery network launched by a telecommunications service provider on the network it owns.

facts.text: Rapid growth of streaming video traffic led telecommunications providers to launch their own CDNs, to lessen demands on the network backbone and reduce infrastructure investment.
Telco CDNs own the last mile and can cache content deep in their networks, minimizing the distance video travels over the general Internet and delivering it more quickly and reliably.
They have a built-in cost advantage, because traditional CDNs must lease bandwidth from telcos and build the operator's margin into their own costs.

Operating their own delivery infrastructure gives operators control over resource utilization and better quality of service, whereas traditional CDNs manage content with little or no knowledge of the operator's network.

title: Virtual CDN
article: Content delivery network#CDN trends > Virtual CDN (vCDN)

definition.text: A virtual CDN, also called a software-defined CDN, uses virtualization to deploy CDN caches dynamically.

facts.text: Virtual CDNs (vCDN), also called software-defined CDNs (sd-CDN), use virtualization to reduce content provider costs while increasing elasticity and decreasing service delay.

Virtual caches are deployed dynamically as virtual machines or containers on physical servers across the provider's coverage, avoiding traditional CDN limits on performance, reliability and availability.
Virtual cache placement depends on both the content type and the server or end-user location, so vCDNs significantly affect service delivery and network congestion.

title: Edge content service protocols
article: Content delivery network#Content networking techniques > Content service protocols

definition.text: Content service protocols give access to content services, such as content adaptation and dynamic page assembly, distributed through a content network.

facts.text: ICAP, developed in the late 1990s, is an open standard for connecting application servers; several protocol suites give access to content services distributed throughout a content network.
The more recent and robust OPES architecture lets service applications run on the OPES processor itself or remotely on a Callout Server.
Edge Side Includes (ESI) is a small markup language for assembling dynamic web content at the edge.
Generated content, from changing catalogs and forums or from personalization, creates a problem for caching systems, and a group of companies created ESI to overcome it.

definition.text: A CDN can add protection against attacks such as DDoS, but it also brings script-injection and privacy risks.

facts.text: A CDN can improve website security, especially against DDoS attacks, and vendors may extend into DDoS protection, web application firewalls and WAN optimization.
CDNs serving JavaScript have been targeted to inject malicious content into pages; Subresource Integrity ensures a page loads only a script whose content matches a hash the site author references.

Providers can profit from analytics and tracking data collected as their scripts load in the customer's browser origin, so CDNs are pointed out as potential privacy intrusions for behavioral targeting.
A website using a CDN may violate the EU's GDPR; in 2021 a German court ruled that sending a visitor's IP address to a CDN violated it.

title: Image CDN
article: Content delivery network#CDN trends > Image Optimization and Delivery (Image CDNs)

definition.text: An Image CDN serves multiple versions of the same image over HTTP depending on the properties of the requesting browser.

facts.text: An Image CDN serves multiple versions of the same image through HTTP, depending on the properties of the requesting browser as determined by the browser or by server-side logic.
An Image CDN generally combines three components: a CDN for fast serving of images, image manipulation and optimization, and device detection.
Image manipulation and optimization can happen on the fly through URL directives, in batch mode through manual upload of images, or fully automatically.
Device detection determines the properties of the requesting browser or device from the User-Agent string, HTTP Accept headers, Client-Hints or JavaScript.

definition.text: Edge computing is a distributed computing model that brings computation and data storage closer to the sources of data, and so to users.

facts.text: Edge computing is any design that pushes computation physically closer to a user, to cut latency compared with running the application in a centralized data center.

It generalizes the CDN idea: CDN nodes at the network edge prefetch and cache content and can customize it, and edge computing extends this by leveraging cloud infrastructure. Early edge services hosted shopping carts, dealer lookup and ad placement.
Data from devices at the edge pushes network bandwidth to the limit when stored and used in cloud data centers, which cannot guarantee acceptable transfer rates and response times.

Placing analytical resources near users increases responsiveness and throughput. Processing locally avoids long transfers: recognizing speech at the edge lets a system send text to the cloud instead of audio, cutting bandwidth.
Failover management is crucial: if a node goes down users should still reach the service. A voice assistant at the edge can keep serving local users during cloud or internet outages.

Distributing logic across nodes introduces new problems: data traveling between nodes needs its own encryption and edge nodes may be resource-constrained, yet keeping data at the edge can improve privacy by sending less sensitive data to the cloud.
Offloading every task to the edge can slow things down because of transfer times between device and node, so the best configuration depends on the workload.

definition.text: Subresource Integrity (SRI) is a W3C recommendation that protects website delivery by validating assets served by a third party, such as a CDN, so they have not been compromised.

facts.text: The page author gives a cryptographic hash of the resource along with its location; the browser compares that hash with one computed from the fetched resource and discards the resource if they do not match.

An integrity value may hold several space-separated expressions, each a hash algorithm name plus a Base64 digest; when several recognized algorithms are given, the browser validates with the strongest.
SRI works with JavaScript files and linked stylesheets.

A resource from a different origin needs CORS for integrity checking: the server must allow access with the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, and the crossorigin attribute makes the browser request it in CORS mode.

definition.text: A distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack makes a machine or network resource unavailable by flooding it with traffic that comes from many different sources.

facts.text: Denial of service is typically done by flooding the target with superfluous requests to overload it and block legitimate ones; the two general forms are attacks that crash services and attacks that flood them.
In a DDoS the flood comes from many sources, often thousands of malware-infected hosts in a botnet, so blocking a single source is not enough and more sophisticated mitigation is needed.

Common DDoS attacks are UDP flooding, SYN flooding and DNS amplification. A SYN flood leaves half-open connections that exhaust the server's available connections, because the forged sender address never replies.
In a reflected attack, forged requests with the victim's spoofed source address go to many computers whose replies flood the victim; amplification magnifies the bandwidth sent to the victim.

An application-layer (layer 7) DDoS over-exercises specific functions, such as search or database access. It needs fewer resources than network-layer attacks, often accompanies them and can look like legitimate traffic.
A yo-yo attack targets cloud applications that autoscale, alternating bursts of traffic that cause a scale-up with pauses that cause a scale-down.

Defense combines attack detection, traffic classification and response tools. Upstream filtering diverts traffic through a scrubbing center that passes only legitimate traffic, since DDoS can overwhelm any hardware firewall.
A sudden spike in popularity, such as a link on a major site, can deny service with the same effect as a DDoS attack, without any attacker.

definition.text: Peer-to-peer (P2P) is a distributed architecture in which participants share part of their own resources, such as processing power, storage or network capacity, directly with other peers.

facts.text: Each peer is both resource provider and requester, with no intermediary; the client-server model instead gives the roles to different participants, with centralized servers providing and clients requesting.
Peers talk directly at the application layer over logical overlay links on top of TCP/IP; overlays handle indexing and peer discovery, and networks are classed as unstructured, structured or hybrid.
Unstructured networks form by random connections, so they are easy to build, allow local optimizations and cope well with churn, peers frequently joining and leaving. Gnutella and Kazaa are examples.

Structured networks impose a topology so any node can efficiently find even a rare resource. The most common type is a distributed hash table, where a variant of consistent hashing assigns each key to a peer.
Hybrid models mix peer-to-peer and client-server, commonly with a central server that helps peers find each other, trading centralized functionality against node equality.

Decentralization removes the single point of failure of client-server systems, and capacity grows as nodes arrive. For content delivery, serving capacity can rise as more users fetch the content, keeping the distributor's cost low.

Peers act as servers as well as clients, so they can be more exposed to remote exploits, and malicious nodes can mount routing attacks such as incorrect lookup routing or corrupting neighbors' routing tables.
P2P systems reach full potential only when many nodes contribute, but many users take without sharing, the freeloader problem, which can in some cases make the community collapse.
